newsitem.title: UK: UK retail sales grow 4.8 percent yr/yr in May-BRC.
newsitem.headline: UK retail sales grow 4.8 percent yr/yr in May-BRC.

text.p: The value of British retail sales grew by 4.8 percent year-on-year in May compared with an upwardly-revised April growth rate of 4.1 percent, the British Retail Consortium (BRC) said on Tuesday.
This compared with growth of 6.2 percent in the year to May 1996.
"Although May was a relatively good month for retailers, there is no sign of a runaway consumer boom," the BRC said.
In the three months to May, retail sales value grew 4.2 percent from the same 1996 period.
The BRC said there was little evidence yet of any general boost from building society windfall bonuses, except perhaps for sales of larger electrical items.
Sales of summer clothing started slowly but benefited from sunny weather at the end of the month, while fresh produce, bread and meat continued to sell strongly but at lower prices than last year.

"May appears to have been a good month for most retail sectors," said Andrew Higginson, chairman of the BRC economic affairs committee. "The month finished on a stronger note but thankfully we are a long way from runaway 'boom' conditions in the high street."
He said retailers accepted the need for recent modest interest rate increases but saw no case for tax rises in the July 2 budget.
Andrew Sentance, chief economic adviser to the BRC, said a number of factors could slow spending growth in the months ahead.
"Recent rises in interest rates will push up mortgage rates and this is likely to hold back the housing market recovery which is supporting some retail sectors," he said.
"If there are tax rises in the Chancellor's forthcoming budget, this would reinforce any slowdown in the growth of spending later this year."
